history: The fourth generation Honda Civic, built on the EF platform, arrived for 1988 as a significant leap forward in size, refinement, and performance. This was the generation where the Civic truly shed its economy-car-only reputation and emerged as a genuinely well-rounded compact car that could compete with the best in its class on nearly every metric.

Honda substantially revised the engine lineup for the fourth generation, introducing the D-series family of engines that would underpin Civic performance for over a decade. The top-spec 1.6-liter unit in the Si produced 108 horsepower — a remarkable figure for a naturally aspirated 1.6-liter engine in 1988 — while the base 1.5-liter offered improved refinement over its predecessor.

The fourth generation also marked the maturation of the Civic Si as a genuine performance car. With 108 horsepower, a close-ratio 5-speed, and a chassis tuned for driver involvement, the EF Si was quick, communicative, and rewarding in a way that few economy cars of the era could match. Its double-wishbone front suspension — borrowed from Honda's sports car program — gave it handling that embarrassed many dedicated sports cars.

The CRX continued alongside the fourth-gen Civic, now in its second generation and more capable than ever. The CRX Si with the same 108-horsepower engine and a sub-2,000-pound curb weight was a genuine sports car bargain that attracted a devoted following. Together, the EF Civic and CRX defined a generation of Honda enthusiasm that continues to resonate deeply with collectors today.
did_you_know: The fourth-gen Civic Si used a double-wishbone front suspension — the same layout found on Honda's NSX supercar — rather than the cheaper strut suspension used by virtually every other economy car of the era. This gave the EF Si handling characteristics that were genuinely sports-car-like and made it a dominant force in autocross competition throughout the late 1980s and early 1990s.

trims.name: Civic DX
trims.description: The base DX trim with the 1.5L carburetor engine, strut front suspension, and the essentials — a practical and reliable daily driver at an accessible price.

trims.name: Civic LX
trims.description: The mid-range LX added air conditioning, power steering, upgraded audio, and improved interior materials over the DX while keeping the 1.5L engine.

trims.name: Civic EX
trims.description: The top standard trim with the fuel-injected 1.6L engine, sunroof, alloy wheels, and a more complete feature set — the sweet spot of the non-Si lineup.

trims.name: Civic Si
trims.description: The performance flagship with the 108hp fuel-injected 1.6L engine, double-wishbone front suspension, close-ratio 5-speed, sport seats, and a body kit that set it apart visually and dynamically.

variants.name: Civic Si (EF)
variants.description: The EF Si remains one of the most celebrated Civics ever built. Its combination of a willing 108hp engine, double-wishbone suspension geometry, precise steering, and light weight created a driving experience that rivaled dedicated sports cars — at economy car prices.

variants.name: Honda CRX Si
variants.description: The second-generation CRX sharing the EF platform produced an almost mythical driving machine. At under 2,000 pounds with 108 horsepower, the CRX Si offered a power-to-weight ratio that made it a terror on back roads and a dominant autocross competitor for years.

variants.name: Civic Wagon RT4WD
variants.description: A genuinely unusual variant — the fourth-gen Civic Wagon was available with a real-time 4-wheel-drive system, making it one of the earliest all-wheel-drive compact wagons ever sold. A quirky but capable niche vehicle that has developed a small but dedicated collector following.
